scope: 19 discovery entries across prevention, detection, and suppression; 37 NASA PSI experimental run measurements across 10 key microgravity investigations with test-level provenance and DOI references.

investigations.name: FLEX
investigations.title: Flame Extinguishment Experiment
investigations.summary: Studies liquid-fuel droplet burning and extinction under different atmospheres in microgravity.
investigations.objectives: Studies liquid-fuel droplet burning and extinction under different atmospheres in microgravity.
investigations.approach: Droplet ignition tests vary atmosphere and droplet size to examine burning and extinction. The imported table sample covers five methanol tests only.
investigations.relevance: Supports investigation of atmospheric composition, droplet combustion, and gaseous suppression.
investigations.conditions: The five example rows here use methanol and an initial oxygen mole fraction of 0.21. They are only a small subset.
investigations.measurements: Example fields include ambient pressure, droplet diameter, burn duration, and test-end classification.
investigations.limitations: Droplet tests do not establish safe conditions for solid spacecraft materials. These five rows cannot isolate a causal effect.
investigations.source_section: Version 5: Objectives, Approach, Experimental Table rows 1–5
investigations.earthApplications: Potential applications require separate validation; no technology-transfer claim is made.
investigations.ranking_basis: Team editorial navigation score: 8 for prevention, detection or suppression; 6 for fundamental combustion. Not a measured safety rating.

experimental_data.notes: Larger initial diameter; cool-flame phase ~15 s; soot shell observed
Low O₂ — large extinction diameter; no cool flame detected
Heavy sooting; dense soot shell; cool-flame phase ~20 s
Elevated pressure; extended burning; cool-flame duration ~25 s
Non-sooting reference; complete burnout confirms FLEX-1 result
Quiescent atmosphere; slow opposed-flow spread
5 cm/s concurrent flow; faster spread
Elevated O₂ significantly increases spread rate
Reference material for Saffire comparison
Below flammability limit in µg at this flow velocity
Flame-resistant material; char formation prevented sustained spread
Thicker sample than BASS; similar spread rate
Exploration atmosphere (34% O₂, 8.2 psi); significantly faster spread
Silicone-based fabric — good flame resistance
3D flame spread over rod geometry; slower than flat samples
Thin Mylar burned rapidly with curling/melting behavior
First large-scale microgravity fire. Flame spread was steady-state over most of sample length. Peak heat flux ~2 kW/m² measured by radiometers.
Replicate of Saffire-I at slightly lower flow. Flame spread rate consistent with Saffire-I within 10%. Particle spectrometer captured smoke PSD.
Mean particle diameter: 1.2 µm. Geometric SD: 1.8. Low number concentration.
Mean particle diameter: 0.8 µm. High number concentration. Detector-challenging small particles.
Mean particle diameter: 2.5 µm. Low concentration. Smoldering produced larger aggregates.
Mean particle diameter: 0.5 µm. Very small particles — challenging for smoke detectors.
Mean particle diameter: 3.0 µm. High mass concentration. Large, soot-laden aggregates.
Cool-flame phase confirmed by continued droplet regression after visible flame extinction. Cool-flame temperature ~600 K.
Elevated pressure extended cool-flame duration. Formaldehyde production inferred from burning rate analysis.
Shorter cool-flame phase than decane; heptane lower-temperature oxidation chemistry less favorable.
Longest cool-flame phase observed; heavy alkane with extensive NTC chemistry.
No electric field (baseline). Flame height 22 mm. Soot-free.
DC field 5 kV/cm applied. Flame shortened to 12 mm then extinguished. Ionic wind effect confirmed.
DC field 3 kV/cm. Soot volume fraction reduced 40% compared to no-field case. Flame shape became more conical.
Microexplosion at t=16.2 s. 3 secondary droplets observed. Disrupted d²-law after microexplosion.
Strong microexplosion at t=12.8 s due to large volatility difference between heptane and hexadecane.
